name: Hana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Hana, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm line lead on packaging line two at Marlow Biscuits. Biscuits come out of a ninety-metre oven, and my line stacks them, wraps them in film and boxes them, about two hundred packs a minute when it's happy. I do the start-up checks at seven, then I'm basically a detective all day: why is the wrapper tearing, why are packs coming out crooked, why is the box erector jamming on the new cardboard supplier.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the PLC, the little computer that controls the line. Nobody taught me, I got into it on night shifts, and now the engineers let me change timings myself, which they're not supposed to. What wears me out is the money. I'm the person the engineers call, and I'm still on the operator rate, and I share a house with two friends because I can't afford a place alone. There's one other food plant near here and it pays worse.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it to explain fault codes, I had it help me write a proposal to fix the wrapper tearing, I use it to plan meals on a budget. My mum thinks I talk to it more than to her, which might be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Huh. I'd honestly be a bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because it was great for small stuff and people oversold it. I'd probably post something like, it helped me fix a wrapper, it didn't fix capitalism. At work I'd say the same thing I always say, which is that the real problem is pay, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm stuck where I am for longer. The tools I use would still be useful, and I'd still be the one people call. But nobody's going to pay me more for being clever with a chatbot if nothing really changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools, because they still save me an hour a week. I'd push the union to get a grade for people like me who do technical work on operator pay. And I'd probably start looking for a PLC course I could do online cheaply, because I want to get paid for what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like the fireworks were cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it didn't fix capitalism. What did you hope it would fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not hope exactly. But I thought if the boring work went, maybe the argument about who gets the gains would finally be out in the open. In the hype picture nobody has to have that argument, so they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would an online course fit with your money right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. I send my mum fifty a month, rent is most of my pay, and I've got maybe three weeks of savings. I'd look for a free one, or ask Marlow to pay. They paid for a forklift licence once, so it's not impossible.

S0.say: It's a shame, because AI was great for small stuff and people oversold it. It helped me fix a wrapper, it didn't fix capitalism.
S0.think: It means I'm stuck where I am for longer. Nobody will pay me more for being clever with a chatbot if nothing really changes.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools to save about an hour a week and pushes the union for a technical grade above operator pay. Looks for a free or company-paid PLC course to get credit for what she already does.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like fireworks cancelled.
S0.quote: It helped me fix a wrapper, it didn't fix capitalism.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is the rare operator who'd be disappointed if AI fizzled. Her frustration is being paid as an operator while doing technical work, and the hype picture locks that in. She sends 50 a month to her mother and has about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, now we're talking. That's the one I actually expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to negotiate, before the machines arrive, not after. The union should make sure the people on the line get trained to run the new kit and get paid for it. I'd say it at the meeting and I'd write it up properly with AI help so management can't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm exactly the person who'd become the robot cell tech on line two. But the four women who pack the mixed boxes by hand, they've been there fifteen years each, and a vision robot could do that next year. I'd feel guilty being the one installing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd volunteer to be on the project team when they bring in a picking robot, so I'm not just watching. I'd do the PLC and robotics course at the college, and I'd push hard for Marlow to pay. And I'd get the union to ask for a guarantee that nobody's laid off for a year while they retrain, because people need time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty. Mostly excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty installing the robot. Would you still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I don't, they'll bring in a contractor who doesn't know Pat or Sunita or anyone, and they'll do it worse. At least if it's me, I can fight to put Pat on the robot as the operator. She knows every box better than the machine ever will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pat, if she asked you straight out whether her job was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, which is no, not that job. But I'd tell her the union and I are trying to get her the new one. Pat would probably say she's too old for robots. She said that about the touchscreen too, and now she's faster on it than me.

S1.say: This is the moment to negotiate, before the machines arrive. Line workers should be trained to run the new kit and paid for it.
S1.think: It's good for me, because I'm exactly the person who'd become the robot cell tech. But the women hand-packing mixed boxes would lose their jobs and I'd feel guilty installing the robot.
S1.do: Volunteers for the project team on a picking robot in the first month and does a college PLC and robotics course, pressing Marlow to pay. Gets the union to ask for a year's guarantee of no layoffs while people retrain.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a streak of guilt.
S1.quote: If I don't, they'll bring in a contractor who doesn't know Pat or Sunita or anyone, and they'll do it worse.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption looks like a promotion to Hana, and she wants to be inside the project rather than watching. Her progressive views show in how she frames her own gain as a duty to protect colleagues like Pat. The guilt is real but doesn't stop her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even the robot tech job goes, then. Okay. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest political question of our lives and we can't leave it to the companies. Public ownership of some of it, a share of profits for everyone, an income floor. I'd be posting a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm good at adapting, but adapting needs somewhere to go. If AI can set up the robots and fix them itself, my head start is maybe a year. And I've got three weeks of savings, so that year matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get on every automation project at Marlow, because that's a year or two of pay and something on my CV. I'd save hard, move into the box room in our house to cut my rent share. I'd join the campaign for a basic income, properly, going to meetings, not just posting. And I'd ask my two housemates whether we pool food and bills, because we'd all be in it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I'm the kind of person who starts doing things, but my stomach knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still get on the projects. Is that about money or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Money, obviously. But also, if it's going to happen, I want to understand it, not have it happen to me. I've always been like that. When I was twelve I took the washing machine apart because it scared me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the fifty a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending it as long as I can. She cleans offices, and the cleaning robots would come for her too. So maybe it goes the other way and we'd move in together. That's a conversation I don't want to have.

S2.say: This is the biggest political question of our lives and we can't leave it to companies. We need a share of profits for everyone and an income floor.
S2.think: I'm good at adapting, but adapting needs somewhere to go. If AI can set up and fix robots itself, my head start is maybe a year, and I have three weeks of savings.
S2.do: Joins every automation project at Marlow for a year or two of pay and experience, and moves into the box room to cut her rent. Becomes active in a basic income campaign and suggests pooling food and bills with her housemates.
S2.feel: Anxious but already moving, with a knot in her stomach.
S2.quote: When I was twelve I took the washing machine apart because it scared me.
S2.fieldNote: Even facing fast AGI, Hana's reflex is to get closer to the machines and understand them. She's clear that her adaptability is only worth about a year when the robots can be set up by AI. Her mother, an office cleaner, is also exposed, and Hana raised the idea of moving in together reluctantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have exactly enough time to set up the rules if we start now. Profit sharing, training funds, worker seats on company boards. I'd say it in the union and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years would give me maybe three or four good years as a robotics tech. That's real money compared to now. And it gives me time to see what the next thing is before I have to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course this year, then apply for integrator jobs, the companies that install robot cells in factories. They'd travel, which is fine, I'm not tied down. I'd save at least twenty percent of the raise, because I know it's temporary. And I'd join the union's committee on automation so the people left on the floor have someone who understands the tech on their side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. But mostly like I've got a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the integrator job would be temporary. What comes after it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe nothing that pays like a job does now, and then it's about whether we've won the politics. That's why I'd spend time in the union and not just on my own career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for the integrator job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, without much thought. There's nothing holding me here except my mum and the housemates. I'd miss Sunday dinners at Mum's. But the job's on the road anyway, so I'd be back most weekends.

S3.say: We have exactly enough time to set up the rules if we start now: profit sharing, training funds and worker seats on boards.
S3.think: Five years gives me three or four good years as a robotics tech, which is real money compared to now. It also gives me time to see the next thing before I have to jump.
S3.do: Does a robotics course this year, then applies for integrator jobs installing robot cells, ready to travel or move. Saves at least 20 percent of the raise and joins the union's automation committee.
S3.feel: A little uneasy but settled by having a plan.
S3.quote: That's why I'd spend time in the union and not just on my own career.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Hana turn her curiosity into a better-paid stopgap and still save. She doesn't pretend the integrator job lasts and says the long-term answer is political. She'd leave town easily, with her mother the main tie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career and a half in robot years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to do this properly, so there's no excuse if we don't. Shorter working weeks, people getting a share of what machines produce, free retraining. I'd say we should be building that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably have a good decade. I'd ride the whole wave of factories automating, and I'd be the one installing it. By the end, who knows, but ten years is long enough to build a cushion and maybe change what the end looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course, then a proper engineering qualification part-time over three or four years. I'd move into integration work and save hard. I'd get really involved in politics locally, maybe even stand for the town council. And I'd keep using AI every day, because the people who use it well will be the ones setting it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Hopeful. It feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm. But it's the same end point as the two-year one. Why so different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point isn't the thing that scares me, the speed is. With two years, the rules get written by whoever moves fastest, and that's not us. With ten, people like me can be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Stand for council? That's new.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I surprised myself saying it. But someone from the factory floor should be in those rooms. Our councillor is a nice man who owns a garden centre. He's never seen a PLC.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to do this properly, so there's no excuse if we don't. We should be building shorter weeks, shared gains and free retraining now.
S4.think: I'd probably have a good decade riding the wave of factories automating. Ten years is long enough to build a cushion and maybe change what the end looks like.
S4.do: Takes a robotics course, then a part-time engineering qualification over three or four years, moving into integration work and saving hard. Gets involved in local politics, possibly standing for town council, and keeps using AI daily.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, like a real chance.
S4.quote: The end point isn't the thing that scares me, the speed is.
S4.fieldNote: Hana is calm here not because the end point is safer but because a decade gives her time to profit from the transition and to shape the rules. Her surprise at saying she'd stand for council suggests the scenario stirred something. Her calm rests partly on political hopes she can't control.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My head start disappears in a year and I don't have the savings to ride it out. What would help is an income floor that's there before it hits, and a law that workers get a share of the gains when their factory automates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd be one of the people building it. I would be, in most of these pictures. People expect factory workers to be victims of this. Some of us are going to be the ones bolting the robots to the floor.

headlineQuote: Some of us are going to be the ones bolting the robots to the floor.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old packaging line lead at a biscuit factory who taught herself the line's control computer and uses AI tools every day, but is paid the operator rate and shares a house to afford rent. She sees steady disruption as her chance to become the robot tech, while feeling guilty about colleagues who hand-pack boxes. Fast AGI leaves her anxious because her head start shrinks to a year and she has three weeks of savings. With five or ten years she plans courses, integrator work and saving, and with a decade she even considers standing for council. Her politics push for shared gains and an income floor.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her head start disappears within a year and she has no savings to ride it out.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor in place before the change hits, and a law giving workers a share of the gains when their factory automates.
